La communauté LGBTQ+ latino-canadienne :: The Latin American Canadian LGBTQ+ Community: Between Activism and Resilience
Nous avons décidé de raconter l’histoire: We decided to tell the stories of three Latin American Canadian members of the LGBTQ+ community
Aujourd’hui, alors que Montréal célèbre: Today, as Montréal celebrates its Pride parade, we decided to tell the stories of three Latin American Canadian members of the LGBTQ+ community, a subject Canadian media don’t cover much.
Il s’agit de Viviana Santibáñez, une fem: They are Viviana Santibáñez, a transsexual woman originally from Mexico who has been an activist for her community for more than twelve years, first in the United States and then in Canada; Daniel Martinez, a gay man also born in Mexico, who began his activism after coming out in Canada; and Liliana Madriz, a gay woman originally from Venezuela who, at 55, began building a new life by accepting herself as a lesbian.
Ces trois personnes aux visions et origi: These three people, with different outlooks and origins, celebrate living in a country that allowed them to recognize, accept and love themselves, but where rejection still exists, even within Latin American Canadian groups themselves.
<strong>Viviana Santibáñez : émigrer, s’: Viviana Santibáñez: emigrating, accepting herself and emigrating again
Viviana Santibáñez milite depuis 12 ans: Viviana Santibáñez has been an activist for the LGBTQ+ community for 12 years. Photo: courtesy of Viviana Santibáñez.
Viviana Santibáñez est née à Tierra Cali: Viviana Santibáñez was born in Tierra Caliente, a region of Mexico considered one of the most dangerous in the country because of the presence of organized crime.
Cette activiste a plusieurs chapeaux dan: This activist wears many hats in her daily life. She works for the inclusion and protection of LGBTQ+ Latinas, and she is an immigration consultant.
Elle émigre à Houston, au Texas, en 2008: She emigrated to Houston, Texas, in 2008, at the age of 14. “My parents decided to send me to the United States. I like to think it’s because they realized that my behaviour and my expressions were different and that I wasn’t fit or safe in that environment,” she explains.
Cette femme élancée aux longs cheveux no: This slender woman with long, jet-black hair and porcelain skin weighs every word. You can tell she wants to find the right ones.
Elle vit pendant dix ans à Houston. C’es: She lived in Houston for ten years. That’s where she began her transition, at 15. She changed the way she dressed and added feminine clothing to her wardrobe. At 16, she started taking hormones without medical supervision.
À 21 ans, elle rencontre un spécialiste: At 21, she met a specialist and continued her transition until she was living her life as a woman, “fully expressing my identity,” she says.
Le discours anti-immigration du présiden: The anti-immigration rhetoric of then-president Donald Trump and the anti-LGBTQ+ positions of the American far right pushed her to go into exile in Canada.
« J’ai pensé qu’il était dangereux pour: “I thought it was dangerous for me to stay in the United States because I’m a trans woman and a woman of colour, but also because when you’re an activist, you become a target. I told myself: this place is no longer safe for me. It’s time to secure my future.”
Viviana moved to Toronto in 2018. She quickly realized that the city offered few services for the LGBTQ+ Latino community, compared with Houston.
Nous l’avons interviewée parce que son t: We interviewed her because her work is crucial at a time when members of the LGBTQ+ Latina community in Canada feel that intolerance has grown among Latinos themselves. Debates and controversies over the LGBTQ+ cause are multiplying within Canada’s Latin American community, and social media is a platform that echoes these disputes.
Elle crée donc l’organisme Vivi’r LGBTQ+: So she founded the organization Vivi’r LGBTQ+ while going through her own asylum claim. “Unlike other asylum seekers, I didn’t have a language barrier. I could do a lot of things, do research,” explains this frank woman with a subtle sense of humour. Her ambition and her altruism within the LGBTQ+ community are such that she dreams of Vivi’r becoming a pan-Canadian organization.
Cinq années se sont écoulées depuis la c: Five years have passed since the creation of Vivi’r, through which Viviana has supported members of the community, especially transgender Latinos. That support ranges from the first steps after arriving in Canada, for those fleeing the homophobia and transphobia they endure in their countries of origin, to how to get medical treatment, including antiretrovirals for HIV.
Pourtant, ce n’est qu’en juillet de cett: Yet it was only in July of this year that Vivi’r was registered as a non-profit organization, “with the help of a non-Latin American law firm,” she specifies, as if to underline the fact that no Latin American firm wanted to support her through the process.
En juin dernier, lorsque l’Ontario a ann: Last June, when Ontario announced that the rainbow flag would fly in institutions such as schools and even the Canadian Parliament, an avalanche of Facebook posts appeared defending “the traditional family created by God.” “I’m not surprised,” Viviana says. She prefers not to spend her time on these debates so she can stay focused on her work.
<strong>Première pierre sur sa route d’a: A first stone on her path as an activist in Canada
Viviana croit que pour servir les causes: Viviana believes that to serve the causes close to her heart, you must first win the support of the Latina community, then network and lobby, before reaching the seats of political power to bring about change through legislation. That is her current strategy.
C’est d’ailleurs ainsi qu’elle a rencont: That is how she met Oscar Vigil, director of the Hispanic Canadian Heritage Council, an Ontario non-profit organization well known to Latin American Canadians, which aims to promote the contribution of Hispanic and Latin American culture to Canadian heritage. Getting accepted within this organization, through her presence at its events, at a celebration of Latino heritage or a networking evening, wasn’t easy, the activist admits.
« Comme toujours, il y a eu des réaction: “As always, there were negative reactions because many people didn’t agree with the LGBTQ+ community being visible. I don’t understand why, when they know Canada has laws that protect the community against discrimination and that those who discriminate face very serious criminal penalties,” she says.
Et ce, en dépit d’une communauté grandis: And this is despite a growing community in a country where freedoms are guaranteed and protected. According to Statistics Canada, the country has about 1 million LGBTQ2+ people, or 4% of the Canadian population aged 15 and over. Of this population, about 52% are women, 44% are men and 3% are non-binary people.
Il n’existe pas de statistiques sur le n: There are no statistics on the number of Latine (*) members of the LGBTQ+ community in Canada, a count that Viviana is currently carrying out.
Actuellement, l’activiste promeut le pro: The activist is currently promoting the program Transchecándome, which empowers and educates transgender women. “Something that isn’t widely known and isn’t talked about is that the transgender community is the most vulnerable, even within the rainbow community. It’s very important to point out that transgender people are always the victims. There is always this machismo among men and among gay men themselves. Because they’re men, they can allow themselves that, it’s what we call patriarchy,” she laments.
Tout ce travail lui a apporté beaucoup d: All this work has brought her a great deal of satisfaction, but the fear never completely goes away. She says she goes to bed every night with a clear mind, satisfied that she has done good. But one question accompanies her almost every day. “What will happen tomorrow? It’s something we have to live with our whole lives, because people have decided to attack us and hate us for who we are. What have we done to them? It seems our only mistake is having been born.”
Daniel Martinez, fondateur de l’organism: Daniel Martinez, founder of the organization Casta Latina. Photo: Pablo Ortiz.
Daniel Martinez, lui aussi mexicain, est: Daniel Martinez, also Mexican, is an ally of Viviana in developing Vivi’r in Montréal. He devotes part of his time to activism, not only for the LGBTQ+ community but also for the Latina community in Quebec, through his own organization, Casta Latina.
À 33 ans, cet ingénieur en aérospatiale: At 33, this aerospace engineer has lived in Canada for seven years. He comes from a modest family in Delicias, a city in the state of Chihuahua. Since childhood, he has been a kind of role model for everyone in the city. He was in fact the first member of his family to earn a university degree, at age 20. At 26, he was recruited by Bombardier.
L’ingénieur, cordial, sensible et éloque: The engineer, cordial, sensitive and eloquent in his manner, arrived in Toronto to take a management position. His colleagues were white men in their forties or fifties. “It was a pretty complicated adjustment. All my colleagues could have been my parents. I arrived in Canada alone and with a very heavy emotional load, because I’d never had the courage to face who I was,” he explains.
Il se consacre donc aux études et au tra: So he threw himself into his studies and his work, a strategy he has applied since childhood.
« Il y a cette idée que dans la grande m: “There’s this idea that in the vast majority of Latin American countries, there are a lot of problems with racism, sexual segregation and homophobia. My family is no exception. I come from a background where religion has a strong influence,” the young man explains in a low voice as we talk in a corner of the Ville de Saint-Laurent library.
Pendant trois ans, Daniel s’applique don: For three years, Daniel worked hard to silence his anxieties through work, putting in days of 15 to 16 hours. Some weeks, he worked up to a hundred hours, he says. His body and mind began to suffer.
« Je suis tombé dans une profonde dépres: “I fell into a deep depression. My life was nothing but monotony. I realized I was carrying a very heavy burden because I was the star of my family. My mother didn’t go to school and my father only finished high school. I have a younger brother I’ve always been afraid of letting down because I’m his role model and I love him with all my heart,” he admits, tears in his eyes.
Sur les conseils d’une amie, Daniel enta: On the advice of a friend, Daniel began therapy in 2019. The process allowed him to finally accept his sexuality. As with Viviana, acceptance wasn’t immediate. Guided by his psychologist, he one day recognized and accepted that he loved men. It was a revelation for him.
Daniel rencontre ensuite son partenaire: Daniel then met his partner Paco, with whom he moved to Montréal. With him, he says with a smile, “I’ve had the three best years of my life. I now see life in colour,” he repeats, his hand on his heart.
Lorsqu’on lui demande s’il remarque une: When asked whether he has noticed an increase in intolerance among Latin American Canadians toward members of the LGBTQ+ community, Daniel chooses to answer with an example: “In June, Pride month in Ontario, my boyfriend posted a photo in a Facebook group created by Latinos in Canada, of a gay couple we’re friends with who adopted a baby. The post generated thousands of comments and the vast majority of them were hateful. So much so that the group’s administrator asked Paco to delete the photo because he himself had received a lot of private messages asking him to do so. It’s very sad, because it’s not only segregation against the LGBTQ+ community, it’s also a limit on freedom of expression,” he adds, visibly upset.
Malgré la haine exprimée dans ce type de: Despite the hatred expressed in this kind of post, Daniel believes he is privileged. In his view, rejection within the Latina community is expressed far more often toward trans people than toward gay people. “I feel loved and respected by everyone. That weighs on me, because even though I’ve accepted myself, yes, I look around, I see everything that’s going on, and I ask myself: why can’t people just accept and respect one another?”
<strong>Commencer une nouvelle vie à la: Starting a new life in her fifties
Liliana Madriz est bien connue de la com: Liliana Madriz is well known in Montréal’s Latin American community. Photo: Pablo Ortiz.
Liliana Madriz habite au Canada depuis v: Liliana Madriz has lived in Canada for twenty-five years. She is well known in Montréal’s Latin American community, especially the Venezuelan community. She is co-owner of one of the city’s most popular Latino restaurants. Her manner is friendly, and she usually accompanies her greetings with a big smile.
Elle est arrivée au Canada à l’âge de 35: She arrived in Canada at 35 and settled in Montréal with her husband and two daughters. Raised in a traditional Venezuelan Catholic family, she lived within that model for twenty years, “unsatisfied,” she says, touching her hands as if trying to reassure herself.
Même si l’idée d’aimer les femmes lui a: Even though the idea of loving women crossed her mind, she dismissed it as quickly as it appeared. “Because of social pressure, I never gave myself the freedom to think I could be gay. Looking back, yes, the idea crossed my mind more than once, but I pushed it away.”
En apparence, sa vie était presque parfa: On the surface, her life was almost perfect. A professional and an entrepreneur, she succeeded in every area. “But I didn’t feel happy. And that’s one of the first things I told my psychologist,” she explains.
Comme Daniel, c’est la thérapie qui lui: Like Daniel, it was therapy that helped her understand part of that dissatisfaction. “It took me three years to accept the reality: it was there, but I wasn’t accepting it,” she remembers.
Changer de vie, c’était comme « se jeter: Changing her life was like “jumping into the void,” an idea that paralyzed her. Therapy helped her understand that she could free herself from her fears, and then she took the step.
« Je me suis acceptée, ce qui signifiait: “I accepted myself, which meant becoming independent and starting a divorce. It was very hard, especially because I kept thinking: who’s going to be interested in me in my fifties?” She absent-mindedly touches a medallion of the Virgin Mary. Is she a believer? She answers bluntly: “Not at all anymore.” Mary has become a symbol of protection, a precious object given by her mother, who lives in Venezuela.
Ce saut dans le vide de Liliana a été un: Liliana’s leap into the void was a very solitary process. In the eyes of all her friends, she explains, she had always been a married woman in a heterosexual couple. “When the separation happened, many of those friends didn’t know where to stand,” she says.
Même si la plupart de ses amis la soutie: Even though most of her friends supported her decision, she then felt the need to build other kinds of relationships. “It’s not the same. You need to talk to someone who’s in your situation. It’s a very solitary and painful process. There’s a mourning to go through,” she repeats.
Elle s’appuie donc sur des applications: So she turned to apps and Facebook groups to begin building a new circle of friends within the LGBTQ+ community, particularly among lesbians. “It wasn’t necessarily to find a partner, but simply to socialize and start making new friends,” she explains.
Dans son commerce, Liliana a remarqué un: At her business, Liliana noticed a slight distance from some customers, but she specifies that there were very few.
Liliana vit désormais en couple avec une: Liliana now lives with a Quebec woman, and with a big smile she says she is happy with her new life.
« Avant, j’avais beaucoup d’anxiété et d: “Before, I had a lot of anxiety and dissatisfaction. I didn’t know why. I thought I had to work more, that I had to change careers, that I had to do something. I was always looking for what I was missing to feel fulfilled. When I accepted myself, all that anxiety disappeared,” she says.
Bien que sa vie et son environnement aie: Although her life and surroundings have changed, she insists she is still the same person. “I’m still María Liliana Madrid, so why should I be looked down on or judged differently if there’s a woman beside me instead of a man?”
À ceux qui agitent encore la controverse: To those who still stir up controversy over other people’s sexual orientation or gender identity, Liliana has a message: “I think you should open your eyes. Don’t be carried away by what someone told you or by what a religion told you or by what conformity dictates. You have to evolve.”
Viviana, Daniel et Liliana son trois per: Viviana, Daniel and Liliana are three people with very different outlooks and experiences, but they have one thing in common: although accepting their gender identity or sexual orientation led to a migration, a change of environment and of social circle, they insist they are the same people in their essence.
Le chemin d’acceptation de leurs choix p: The path toward accepting their personal choices seems to be widening in Canadian society, thanks to the laws that protect them. But, in their own words, that doesn’t mean they don’t run into obstacles from time to time.
